title: Surface charges in a Rydberg atom-nanowaveguide hybrid quantum system
authors: Aswathy Raj, Anna Kortel, Krishna Jadeja, Dylan J. Brown, Alexey Vylegzhanin, Robert Löw, Síle Nic Chormaic
abstract: Hybrid quantum platforms based on highly excited Rydberg atoms coupled to nanophotonics devices offer a promising route toward scalable quantum networks and integrated quantum technologies. However, the close proximity of Rydberg atoms to dielectric nanostructures makes these systems particularly susceptible to uncontrolled surface electric fields that can lead to a degradation of the excitation process. Here, we experimentally investigate Rydberg excitation of laser-cooled $^{87}$Rb atoms via the evanescent field of an optical nanofiber in the presence of fiber-guided red- and blue-detuned light fields as used to trap ground state atoms in fiber-based dipole traps. We observe a time evolution of the Rydberg excitation spectrum when both the dipole trapping fields are on and the additional spectral features that appear can be suppressed by applying an external oscillating electric field to the system, strongly indicating that surface charge accumulation is responsible for the observed spectral feature. The experimental results are reproduced qualitatively by a model that incorporates DC energy level shifts arising from electric fields generated by charges deposited on the nanofiber surface. We identify Rydberg-ground state collisional ionization, which is enhanced by the dipole trapping fields, as the dominant mechanism for charge generation. These results provide new insight into charge dynamics at dielectric nanophotonic interfaces and establish practical guidelines for mitigating surface charge-induced electric fields in fiber-integrated Rydberg quantum systems.
summary: The authors experimentally investigate how surface charge accumulation on an optical nanofiber degrades the excitation of Rydberg atoms in a hybrid quantum system. They demonstrate that spectral splitting is caused by DC electric fields from these charges, which are generated via enhanced collisional ionization. The results provide crucial guidelines for designing and operating robust fiber-integrated quantum devices.
main_problem: The study investigates how uncontrolled surface electric fields, arising from charge accumulation on dielectric nanostructures, degrade Rydberg excitation processes in hybrid quantum systems.
main_result: Spectral deformations and splitting observed in the Rydberg excitation spectrum are strongly attributed to DC energy level shifts caused by accumulated surface charges. Applying an external oscillating electric field can suppress these spectral features.
method: The research combines experimental measurements of time-dependent Rydberg spectra with theoretical modeling using master equations incorporating static electric field shifts.
model_or_system: The system involves laser-cooled $^{87}	ext{Rb}$ atoms excited to high-lying Rydberg states near an optical nanofiber (ONF). The model incorporates DC energy level shifts ($\delta_{DC}$) derived from surface charges, which are generated primarily through enhanced Rydberg-ground state collisional ionization.
key_observables: Time evolution of the Rydberg excitation spectrum; spectral splitting/deformation magnitude; remaining MOT population ($N_2$).
important_parameters: Rydberg states (e.g., $35D_{5/2}, 40D_{5/2}$); electric field strengths ($\sim 1-2.5 	ext{ V/cm}$); collisional ionization rate ($\Gamma_{	ext{coll}}$).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the observed spectral changes are due to static DC shifts from surface charges, which can be mitigated by external AC fields.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate schematic setups, time evolution of spectra showing deformation (Figs. 2, 3), comparison with model predictions based on field strength (Fig. 5), and the dependence of spectral features on laser polarization alignment (Figs. 11, 12).
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the physical platform and observing time-dependent spectral changes to modeling these shifts using DC electric fields derived from charge generation mechanisms like collisional ionization, culminating in guidelines for mitigation.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it addresses a critical practical limitation—surface noise—in scaling up integrated quantum technologies utilizing Rydberg atoms near solid-state waveguides. It provides quantitative methods to characterize and mitigate environmental decoherence sources.
